_readme: Mutation evidence a target's acceptance quotes, kept executable (🎯T32).
A target's acceptance says 'reintroducing X makes test T RED'. That sentence
is quoted once, in a commit message, and then never re-run. Any later commit
that changes T's inputs can retire the evidence without turning anything red:
🎯T30's 8c5e04a added a `landed` argument to ensureSubmitted and passed
landed=true at 🎯T28's call sites, which was correct for the branch it modelled
and weakened no assertion — but it made 🎯T28's over-broadness mutation stop
biting TestT28DailyDeliveredFramesReportSuccess. Every suite stayed green.
This file is the machine-readable form of those sentences, and
scripts/check-mutation-evidence.py re-derives them: `make verify-mutation-evidence`,
part of `make gate` on Colossus. GitHub Actions is not used. Each entry names the target, the mutation as an anchored source edit,
and the tests that must go RED (and the ones that must stay GREEN) under it.
The same Makefile target also runs the check with --prove-teeth, which is what
keeps THIS check from becoming the next unwired oracle: an entry may declare a
`decay`, and --prove-teeth asserts that applying it leaves every suite green
(so the hermetic suite sees nothing) while making a `red` test survive the mutation (so this
check, and only this check, goes red).
TO ADD AN ENTRY when you quote mutation evidence in a commit body:
target    the target whose acceptance quotes it
mutation  a stable id for this mutation, unique within the target
what      one line: what the mutation reintroduces or removes
quoted_by the commit whose message quotes this evidence
package   the Go package the tests live in
edits     [{file, find, replace}] — `find` must occur EXACTLY ONCE in file.
Anchor text, not a diff hunk: a hunk decays on the first refactor
of its context. When the anchor stops matching the check goes RED
and says so, which is the point — the mutation must be re-derived
by a human, never silently skipped.
tests     [{name, expect}] — name is a `go test` path, so a subtest is
'TestX/subtest_name'. expect is 'red' (the mutation must kill it)
or 'green' (it must survive — that is how a commit body's
'fixture Y stays green under this mutation, so the two cover
distinct mechanisms' claim stays true).
decay     optional {what, models, edits} — an edit to the TESTS' inputs,
modelled on a real commit, that disarms this evidence without
turning any suite red. --prove-teeth applies it and requires
exactly that: green everywhere on its own, and a `red` test
surviving the mutation once both are applied. Worth declaring
for any entry whose evidence has decayed once already.
go_flags  optional extra `go test` flags, e.g. ["-race"] for a mutation
only the race detector can see. They add to the run, never
redefine it: -run, -v and -count belong to the harness and an
entry naming one is RED (see baseline() in the script).
note      optional prose: provenance, or what decayed here before.

entries.what: Agent.Send drops the provider's error and returns nil, the swallow that made a lost submit invisible above agent.go
entries.note: 2017074 also quoted TestClaudeSendReportsUnsubmittedTurnThroughRealTmux against this mutation. It is not listed here because it skips without tmux and a skipped test is not evidence; the hermetic one holds the contract in every environment.

entries.what: MatchTurnInProgress forgets Claude Code's activity line, so a running turn with a drained composer reads as no chrome at all

edits.find: return turnInProgressHint.Match(f) || spinnerLine.Match(f)

decay.what: the Send-level call site passes landed=true, so sawContent starts true and 🎯T30's composerEmptyIdle branch returns nil before the 🎯T28 classification is consulted at all
decay.models: 8c5e04a, which did this to TestT28DailyDeliveredFramesReportSuccess: correct for the paste branch that test models, no assertion weakened, every suite green, and the caller-visible half of 🎯T28's evidence gone

edits.find: if err := ensureSubmitted(d, false); err != nil {
edits.replace: if err := ensureSubmitted(d, true); err != nil {

entries.note: This is the entry 🎯T32 was filed over. aa71680 quoted TestT28DailyDeliveredFramesReportSuccess/frame_daily_spinner_empty_composer.txt as the caller-visible RED half. 8c5e04a passed landed=true at that call site and the subtest went green under the mutation, leaving only the classifier half biting; 9944f39 restored the contract on the landed=false path as TestT28DeliveredFramesReportSuccessWithoutLandedEvidence, which is what this entry names. The green expectation is aa71680's own distinctness claim: the queued frame is the half 2017074 already closed, so the two fixtures cover different mechanisms rather than doubling up.

edits.find:
case queuedMessagesHint.Match(body):
		return composerQueued

entries.what: MatchUnsubmittedPaste asks whether the composer was DRAWN rather than whether it HOLDS anything, the pre-fix predicate that reported delivered sends as stuck chips

edits.find: return pasteExpandHint.Match(f) && composerHoldsUnsubmitted(frame)

entries.what: maybeContinueGoal stops calling Send, so an open Goal dies after one terminal turn
TestHermeticTaskRunSuccess bounds its run with a 10s context deadline again — the wall-clock bound that let a loaded machine, not the product, decide the verdict

edits.find:
ctx := t.Context()
	events, err := task.Run(ctx, "summarize")
edits.replace:
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10000000000)
	defer cancel()
	events, err := task.Run(ctx, "summarize")

entries.note: The deadline is spelled as a bare 10000000000 so the mutation needs no new import; the guard matches the context.WithTimeout call, not the literal. TestHermeticTaskRunSuccess is listed green on purpose: on an idle machine the restored deadline still passes, which is exactly why this flake stayed citable-green between failures and why the guard, not the test, holds the contract.

entries.what: WaitForResponse arms no silence wake at all, so a turn whose terminal event never arrives has nothing to end it — the unbounded park itself

edits.find: silence := a.after(bound.effective)

entries.note: The red test is structural on purpose. A missing wake is invisible to a behavioural test — it shows up as a HANG, which is the original defect's own signature and costs a test timeout to see (the report that opened 🎯T96 was a 10m panic). Arming the wake before the subscription gives the guard a happens-before point, so the absence is a fast failure instead of a dead suite. The green test is load-bearing: the death wake is a separate mechanism and still answers with no silence timer on the clock at all. Anchor re-derived by hand at 🎯T103: 43fec82 made the wait arm bound.effective rather than bound, so `silence := a.after(bound)` stopped matching and this evidence stopped biting. The mutation it models is unchanged — arm no silence wake at all — and was re-verified against the new text before the anchor was moved.

entries.what: markDead records the death but closes nothing, so the alive flag flips where no waiter can see it and a wait on that agent keeps waiting for an event nothing will publish
entries.note: TestWaitForResponseEndsWhenTheAgentDies fails FAST under this mutation rather than hanging, and that is by design: it drives the clock past its own bound, so an unobserved death is reported as ErrTurnAbandoned — the wrong verdict, available in milliseconds — instead of parking. The green test shows the silence bound cannot cover for the death wake: it never involves a live agent, so it is blind to this mutation.

entries.what: the wait counts only published events as turn activity, so a tmux turn that is plainly working — the TUI repainting its spinner — is convicted as silent because its tool call wrote nothing to the transcript
entries.note: The two activity sources are independent claims and this pins them apart: events still rearm the bound under this mutation, so the green test cannot see it. A bound that only watched the transcript would fire on exactly the longest healthy turns — a Claude tool call emits no JSONL between tool_use and tool_result, however long the tool runs.

entries.what: WaitForResponse goes back to subscribing for future events only, so the turn a blocking submit has already consumed is dropped on the floor — the park that took the root package's 10m alarm
entries.note: The mutation is the differential run that identified 🎯T98: the handover disabled, everything else — the latch, the arming in Send, the recording in publishEvent — left in place, so what goes red is the handover and nothing else. TestWaitForResponseIgnoresEventsFromBeforeTheSubmit is declared green on purpose: it holds the other half of the contract, that the latch never hands back a turn from before the submit, and a mutation that simply deleted the latch would satisfy it trivially. It staying green is what makes the red ones evidence about the handover rather than about the latch existing at all.

entries.what: the read loop names the oversized frame but abandons the stream mid-line, so the next read returns the tail of that frame instead of the next message — the 🎯T661 defect with a better error message

edits.replace:
case len(line)+len(chunk) > MaxLineLen:
			return nil, frameTooLarge(len(line) + len(chunk))

entries.note: The green test is load-bearing, not decoration: it never crosses the cap, so it stays green under this mutation and shows the red ones are pinning the skip specifically, not any breakage of the reader. The red tests overshoot the cap by 3x MaxLineLen on purpose. An earlier fixture overshot by 7 bytes and this mutation SURVIVED it, because a frame that exceeds the cap inside the final read buffer is consumed to its terminator by the read that notices — a false green the sizes now exclude.

entries.what: EncodeEventWire marshals the event without bounding it, so a screenshot tool_result is handed to the wire as a frame over the line cap — the producer half of the same incident
entries.note: The green test holds the other half of the contract: an unbounded codec still relays an ordinary event byte for byte, so it cannot distinguish the two codecs and the red tests are what pin the bound.

entries.what: bounding treats its own conservative budget as the wire's cap: a payload over the budget with nothing long enough to elide is relayed with Raw set to nil, although the frame it would have produced is legal — data thrown away to protect a limit that was never in danger

edits.find:
ev.Raw, ev.Text = raw, text
	ev.Truncated = ev.Truncated || rawCut || textCut

entries.note: This is the defect the adopted branch shipped with, and the two green tests are why it survived its own suite: every other fixture in broker_bound_test.go carries a base64 string far over maxWireStringBytes, so elision always reaches it and the discard branch is never taken. Only a payload whose size is in its shape — hundreds of small strings, none of them long — lands in the gap between the budget (MaxLineLen/2) and the frame ceiling, and there the bound deleted a payload the wire would have carried. The second green test holds the other side of the same boundary: past the ceiling with nothing elidable, dropping Raw is still the right answer, so the red test is pinning where the line sits and not whether there is one.

entries.what: the silence bound stays the configured one whatever deadline the wait is living under, so a thirty-minute bound inside a ten-minute test binary is a diagnosis the process-wide panic always reaches first — the defect 🎯T103 was filed for, and the state 🎯T96's fix left behind
entries.note: The two green tests are the point of this entry, not padding. TestWaitForResponseAbandonedTurnFailsNamingWhatItSaw is 🎯T96's own acceptance and it survives the mutation untouched — which is how the defect shipped green in the first place: 🎯T96 drove every one of its waits from a ManualClock, so the wall-clock deadline of the binary around them was invisible to all eight. TestAWaitOnAManualClockIgnoresTheProcessDeadline stays green for the same structural reason and holds the other side of the line: a manual-clock wait must NOT take this deadline, so the repair cannot be 'shorten everywhere'.

entries.what: a bound shortened by a deadline reports its conviction exactly as one that ran the measured thirty minutes: `make live` uses -timeout 30m, so a live test starting late in that binary is handed a bound under the 2m34.2s of measured healthy Cursor silence and calls a working turn abandoned, with nothing in the error to say the wait ran out of process rather than out of patience

edits.find: func (b turnBound) cut() bool { return b.effective < b.configured }
edits.replace: func (b turnBound) cut() bool { return false }

entries.note: TestAConvictionUnderTheConfiguredBoundClaimsNoCut must stay green here, and that is what stops the repair degenerating into 'always say it was cut': an error that cried cut-short on every abandoned turn would carry no information and would bury the Config.TurnSilenceBound lever a consumer with legitimately slower turns needs. The mutation silences one side of that distinction; the green test holds the other.

entries.what: the process deadline is applied to an agent whose timers run a ManualClock, so a bound measured in manual-clock time is shortened by how long the test BINARY has been running — every silence verdict in the package becomes a function of how far into the suite it ran, which is the 🎯T33 / 🎯T92 / 🎯T93 family rebuilt one layer up
entries.note: Only the guard's own test is declared red, and the omission is deliberate. The other ManualClock waits in this package would still pass under this mutation in a FRESH binary — half of a full -timeout is far longer than their one-minute fixtures — and would begin failing only deep into a long run. That is precisely the hazard, and it is also why they cannot be cited as evidence here: a test whose colour under the mutation depends on how much of the binary's budget is left is not evidence of anything. The green declared instead is the pure arithmetic, which the mutation cannot reach.

entries.what: initialize is handed the same bound the hermetic test shortens, so the earlier handshake step is armed against an assertion about the later one — 🎯T93's defect exactly as it stood before 02cec52 split the bound in two

edits.find: }), codexAppServerInitializeTimeout)

entries.note: TestHermeticCodexThreadStartTimesOut — the test 🎯T93 is ABOUT — is deliberately not declared here, and that omission is the whole finding. It stays GREEN under this mutation on an idle host, because initialize answers at once and only the hanging thread/start reaches the 200ms bound; it goes red only when the host is slow enough for the shared bound to expire on the earlier step. A test whose colour under the mutation is a function of load is not evidence, which is exactly the defect being guarded, and is why the oracle had to move off behaviour and onto the wiring. cl-t33 measured the same thing from the other side: the pre-fix code passed 5/5 at load 44. The declared green is 02cec52's declaration guard, which sees a declared var shortened by a declared test and passes — load-bearing, because it shows the red test pins the step-ordering property specifically and not merely 'something about bounds changed'.

entries.what: Prompt arms the opening-prompt silence watch on a client with no peer wake path, so the wait's verdict is fixed before it starts (🎯T91's defect as it stood before e18806d)

edits.find: watch := !c.firstDone && c.peerWoke != nil

entries.note: The green is 🎯T83's oracle on a transport-owning client, where the watch arms under both the fix and the mutation. That shows the red pins the wake-path condition specifically, not the watch as a whole. When claudia-po hand-ran this at e18806d it also turned TestACPSteerPromptIDStack and TestT50_2PromptAcceptedBeforeWriteAndPermissionBeforeReply red, in 0.00s: awaitPeerActivity's own nil-wake guard turns the old hang into a fast failure. Those two are not declared, because they bite through that second line of defence and not through this condition.

entries.what: awaitPeerActivity loses its `if ch == nil { return report() }` guard, so a client with no wake channel parks for the whole bound on a nil channel
entries.note: The pair shows the two defences are independent. Prompt's arming condition still keeps an unwatchable client out of the wait, so the caller-level test stays green, and only the wait-level test attributes the regression to awaitPeerActivity. When claudia-po hand-ran this at e18806d, the red was the package's 10m timeout panic, because the test measured elapsed time only after the call returned. 41697da bounds the call at 2s so this entry costs seconds under `make gate`.

entries.what: the opening-prompt silence watch never arms (`watch := false`), which is 🎯T83's guarantee gone. This checks that 🎯T91's narrowing of the arming condition did not quietly do the same

edits.find: watch := !c.firstDone && c.peerWoke != nil

entries.note: This is the most load-bearing of 🎯T91's mutations: it is the one that proves the 🎯T83 oracles still see the watch after 🎯T91 narrowed when it arms. The green is 🎯T91's own no-wake-path test. That path never arms the watch, so the test is indifferent to this mutation, and the reds belong to 🎯T83's mechanism, not to 🎯T91's.

entries.what: awaitPeerActivity's outcome never reports the transport closed, so a dead peer is indistinguishable from a silent one and the caller would re-deliver to it

edits.find: closed:   closed,

entries.note: The recipe as recorded in 🎯T91's attestation declared TestCursorStuckPromptWaitEndsWhenTransportDies GREEN here, "because it discards the outcome". It does not stay green, and did not at e18806d either. awaitPeerActivity's loop exits on report()'s own closed field (`out.spoke || out.closed`), so an outcome that stops reporting the close also stops ending the wait. The 🎯T83 test's 3s poll then goes red, as it should. Re-derived at 41697da (cl-t95): both transport-closed tests are red. The assertion gap the recipe described is real, since the 🎯T83 test never reads the outcome, but this mutation cannot show it. The green control is instead the spoke side of the same outcome: the peer-spoke path never reads the closed field, so it stays green. That shows the reds pin the closed report specifically, not the outcome as a whole. Before cl-t95 bounded TestAwaitPeerActivityReportsTransportClosed, its red was the package's 10m timeout panic, which this check reads as no result.

entries.what: ensureAuth reads the shared probe cache without p.mu, so concurrent 401s race the first writer's publish (ENT-001)

edits.find:
p.mu.Lock()
	probe := entry.probe
	p.mu.Unlock()

entries.note: The first entry that needs go_flags. No assertion can see this mutation: authMu still serializes Authorize, so the burst still authorizes once and every request still gets 200. Only the race detector reports the unsynchronized read, which is why ENT-001 was found by the CI -race job rather than by a failing assertion. Nor does the lock make the probe run once. Two 401s can both read nil and both probe; the lock stops them racing on the pointer, and the nil re-check keeps the first writer's pointer. So probe-count is no oracle either, and -race is the only one. Measured by hand at 86e49f9, before this entry existed: 20/20 -count=1 runs red. That is why -count=1 is enough here. The write-side mutant (publish outside p.mu) is deliberately not declared: it failed 3/20 at -count=1, too flaky for a standing gate. The green control is the same upstream and probe stub with a single request. It walks the mutated read serially and stays green, which shows the red is about concurrency and not a broken path.

entries.what: TestHermeticCursorTaskRun bounds its run with a 15s context deadline again, the root-package twin of the 🎯T33 defect: a clock handed to the product through Task.Run that a loaded host can expire before the fake CLI answers

edits.find: ch, err := task.Run(t.Context(), "Reply with exactly: pong")
edits.replace:
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 15000000000)
	defer cancel()
	ch, err := task.Run(ctx, "Reply with exactly: pong")

entries.note: The same shape as 🎯T33's codex entry, one package up, because the root package is where 🎯T33's guard never looked. TestHermeticCursorTaskRun is green on purpose: on an idle host the restored deadline still passes, which is why only the guard can hold this. The deadline is a bare 15000000000 so the mutation needs no new import.

entries.what: The must-not-return window in agent_test.go loses its 🎯T97 exemption marker, so a clock that is still defensible is no longer answered for in source

edits.find: // 🎯T97 exemption: expiry is the PASS, the one shape 🎯T31 allows.
edits.replace: // Expiry is the PASS, the one shape 🎯T31 allows.

entries.note: Pins that an exemption is a marker the guard reads, not prose it forgives: the reasoning is unchanged and the guard still goes red, because an unmarked clock is an unanswered one. The green control is 🎯T93's product-bound guard, the other half of the pair, which does not read test clocks at all.

entries.what: TestCursorACPCloseKillsAfterReadLoopClosed polls under a 2s deadline built from time.Now() again, the 🎯T106 spelling of a wall clock deciding a hermetic verdict: no banned constructor is called, and a loaded host still expires it before the killed process is gone
entries.note: The restored loop calls none of 🎯T97's six constructors, so this entry is red only because 🎯T106's data-flow check follows time.Now() into deadline and reports the .Before. The 2s is spelled 2000000000. wallclockguard stays imported through the file's other uses, so the red is the guard, not a build failure. The green control is 🎯T93's product-bound guard, which does not read test clocks.

entries.what: promptWatchingForSilence takes the second wait's activity snapshot after the session/cancel write instead of at the stack swap, so an answer to the abandoned delivery that lands in between redeems the turn yet counts as silence, and Prompt reports ErrCursorPromptStuck for a turn already answered

edits.find:
c.afterReissueCancel()
	}

entries.note: The racing sibling TestCursorReissueKeepsAReplyRacingTheRedelivery also goes red under this mutation, but only when the host delays the reply past the old snapshot (17/20 at load ~200, gate 3acac48b), so it is not listed: a verdict the host decides is not evidence. The cancellation-ack test stays green because its peer answers only after the re-delivery, after either snapshot, so the two cover distinct mechanisms.
